title: Does an automated coder's error differ across languages, and how much does that move group comparisons?
lede: does an automated coder's error differ across languages? On 44,485 real tweets in Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin and Yoruba, an English word-list coder and an English-trained classifier read almost none of the negative sentiment in Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba (sensitivity 0.4–11%), flipping some language gaps' sign (Hausa–Yoruba +10.6 points true, −6.5 reported); PPI keeps coverage at 93–96% but is never narrower than hand-coding. Not an LLM (no key)
summary: NaijaSenti tweets (Muhammad et al. 2022) in Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin and Yoruba carry native-speaker sentiment labels, so the true negative share of each language (0.22 to 0.60) and every between-language gap is known. Three automated coders stand in for an LLM, which the session could not run: an English word list, a naive-Bayes classifier trained on English GoEmotions comments, and one trained on 19,065 of the Nigerian tweets with a single global threshold. The word list and the English classifier have sensitivity 0.004–0.108 on Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba and 0.09 and 0.39 on Pidgin, whose vocabulary is largely English-derived. Naive coded-share gaps are therefore wrong: Hausa–Yoruba is +0.106 by human labels and −0.065 by the English classifier, Igbo–Yoruba +0.035 against −0.052, and the in-language classifier overstates Hausa–Igbo at +0.293 against +0.071. Naive intervals cover the true gap 0 times in 500 draws for every pair and coder. Prediction-powered inference with 400 hand-coded tweets covers 93–96% but is 0.4–26% wider than hand-coding alone, since the coders are nearly uninformative. Limits: no LLM was run, so nothing here says how a frontier model reads these languages; language is confounded with topic and period; the hand-coded sample is random over the pooled corpus, not stratified by language.
